claim: A fireball erupts from a point, a turbulent ball of flame expanding and rolling outward from a white-hot core to red flame tongues at the rim — looping.

q1_defects.answer: Nothing broken, misaligned, cut off, or blocky. The fireball is centered, fully in frame, high-contrast against the dark surround in every frame, with soft organic edges — no slab shelves, no tile/lattice grid, no mirror seams, no jagged edges. Photoreal-bar check passes: bandingScore stays under the 0.25 visibility threshold on every frame (max 0.246 on play-2, 0.151 on play-1), and visually the volume is a smooth rolling ball, not stacked cards. No console or network errors.
evidence: metrics: bandingScore play-1=0.151, play-2=0.246, play-3=0.238 — all < 0.25 visible-banding threshold

q2_reads_as.answer: Yes — it reads as a fireball. play-1.png shows a large turbulent ball of flame with a white-hot core and orange-to-deep-red tongues at the rim, exactly as claimed; play-2/play-3 show the loop's compressed glowing-ball phase in the same fire palette. Measured dominant warm hue on the burst frame is 37 deg at sat 0.46 with warmFrac 0.87 — inside fire's 10-45 deg band and matching the fire-flame ground truth (play frames hue 37-43 deg). No pink ring, no cream/olive body, no warm-to-cool ACES drift. The cool effHue readings on play-2/3 (~261-267 deg) are background-dominated measurements of the alpha-0 surround; the frames themselves show an unmistakably warm orange/white fireball.
evidence: metrics: play-1 effHue=37, effSat=0.46, warmFrac=0.87 — fire band, matches ground truth
metrics: ground-truth fire-flame play-2 effHue=37, play-1 effHue=43 — same band as fireball-burst play-1

q3_discoverable.answer: Yes. All three labeled controls do something visible and sensible across their range with no instruction needed: turbulence low gives a smooth glowing ball while turbulence high breaks the surface into licking flame detail; scale high reveals fine turbulent tongues vs the diffuse ball at scale low; burstRate registers a change (luma 13.3 -> 14.6 low-to-high, changed=true) though as a rate control its effect is subtler in a still frame.
evidence: control: burstRate low->high changed=true, meanLuma 13.3->14.6; turbulence changed=true; scale changed=true

q4_responsive.answer: Responsive. The play frames show real motion — the ball erupts into a large turbulent burst then rolls back down (frameDeltaMag 13.28 and 17.34 across play-1/play-2), and every control applied with a visible result in ~570ms. The only soft spot is play-2->play-3 (frameDeltaMag 0.58), a slow phase of the loop where two consecutive captures look nearly identical.
evidence: metrics: control latencyMs 565-582 across all 9 sweep captures

q5_net.answer: PLEASED. 'That's a proper fireball — white-hot middle, orange flames curling around the edge, and the sliders actually change how wild it looks.' It looks like a movie explosion frame, not a game sprite, and nothing is broken or confusing.
evidence: metrics: play-1 effHue=37 warmFrac=0.87, bandingScore max 0.246 < 0.25

flags.note: During the loop's recovery phase the ball reads as a smooth featureless glowing orb rather than turbulent flame, and motion nearly stalls there — a user watching closely might find that beat of the loop a little static. Taste call, not a defect.
flags.evidence: fireball-burst/after/play-3.png : metrics play-3 frameDeltaMag=0.58 vs 13-17 on the burst frames

flags.note: burstRate's visible effect in a still capture is subtle (luma 13.3->14.6 low-to-high); it measurably changes the render but a user may need to watch the motion to feel it. The other two controls carry discoverability.
flags.evidence: control: burstRate low->high changed=true, meanLuma 13.3->14.6, frames control-burstRate-low.png vs control-burstRate-high.png
